questions.question: What does the term pret-a-porter mean?
questions.solution_html:
• ANSWER: Prêt-à-Porter is a French word for Ready-to-Wear. Prêt-à
  • Porter is high-quality, factory-made fashion. These sets are available in
  • a variety of sizes to accommodate a large number of consumers. While
  • they differ in price and quality, the unifying feature is that these
  • collections are designed within the limits of standardized sizing.
  • Introduction: A new style is born through innovation. Styles are
  • unique and expensive. Only fashion innovators and leaders wear
  • them.
  • Sheath silhouettes: Silhouette which hugs the body from top to bottom.
  • This silhouette looks best on the women with no too few curves and is
  • generally recommended by slimmer women with well-defined waist.
  • Real or actual or tactile texture: is the real thing. It is the actual way
  • a surface feels when it is felt or touched, such as rough, smooth, soft
  • hard, silky, slimy, sticky, etc. 3-D art such as sculpture and
  • architectural structures are tactile because they can be felt
questions.final_answer: architectural structures are tactile because they can be felt
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: What is mean by scale in proportion?
questions.solution_html:
• ANSWER: Proportion is sometimes referred to as scale. Every design
  • should be composed of shapes and spaces related without too great
  • difference or too much similarity. No shape should be so dominant that
  • all others are insignificant, no background space should be entirely
  • ignored.
  • Rise: The style gains public visibility. Fashion leaders and
  • trendsetters adopt it. Manufacturers increase production. Prices
  • become more accessible.
  • A-line silhouette: The silhouette resembles the capital A which is fitted
  • at top and flares at the skirt. This garment flatters mostly every body type.
  • Garment of this type is narrow at the top and gradually widens towards the
  • hem smoothing out the lines. It best fits every body type
  • Visual or implied texture: Texture: This type of texture is created
  • through visual cues, such as lines, shapes, colors, and patterns, to give
  • the impression of texture without the actual physical feel. Artists use
  • techniques like shading, cross-hatching, and stippling to create the
  • illusion of texture on a two-dimensional surface.
questions.final_answer: Option line silhouette: The silhouette resembles the capital A which is fitted

questions.question: What is Draping?
questions.solution_html:
• ANSWER: Draping is a fundamental technique in fashion design that
  • involves skillfully manipulating cloth on a dress form to create garment
  • prototypes. Unlike flat pattern-making, which begins with 2D designs
  • draping begins with a 3D approach, allowing designers to directly
  • experiment with how cloth interacts with the body's contours and
  • movements. This hands-on approach allows designers to experiment
  • with various folds, pleats, and shapes before finalizing the design
  • through fabric positioning and pinning.
  • Decline: Consumers grow tired of the style. Sales start to slow
  • down. Retailers mark down prices to sell stock. Fashion
  • followers are the last to wear the trend.
  • Empire silhouette: The silhouette with raised waistline. It is fitted top
  • garment and flares under the chest. It is best suited with people not having
  • defined waist. It should be avoided by hourglass and can be worn by both
  • pear and apple figures
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: How does Symmetrical balance differ from Asymmetrical balance?
questions.solution_html:
• balance?
  • ANSWER: Symmetrical Balance (or Formal Balance) is achieved
  • when both sides of a design are identical or very similar, essentially a
  • mirror image, creating an impression of stability and formality.
  • Asymmetrical Balance (or Informal Balance) is achieved when the two
  • sides of a design are not identical, but they still appear visually balanced
  • due to a careful arrangement of elements of different sizes, shapes, or
  • colours. This approach offers more freedom of expression, creates
  • intrigue, and is often used to correct the appearance of body
  • irregularities.
  • Obsolescence: The style is completely rejected. It is considered
  • outdated and unfashionable. The cycle ends for that specific
  • style. A new trend replaces it.
  • Bell or Ball gown silhouette: The Ball Gown or Bell-Shaped dress is
  • generally fitted till waist and gradually widens towards hemline forming a
  • shape like bell-shaped skirt. This style is flattering on almost any body
  • type, but is especially flattering for petite women, or those with small
  • waists. On a pear-shaped woman, the full skirt can do much to camouflage
  • large hips.

questions.question: What do Vertical Lines represent in design?
questions.solution_html:
• ANSWER: Vertical lines in design are used to convey a sense of
  • strength, stability, and formality. They guide the eye up and down
  • which can visually elongate the figure, making the wearer appear
  • taller and slimmer. In fashion and architecture, they reinforce the idea
  • of power and structure due to their rigid, upright nature.
questions.final_answer: of power and structure due to their rigid, upright nature

questions.question: How do straight lines contribute to harmony?
questions.solution_html:
• ANSWER: Straight lines contribute to harmony in a design by helping
  • to establish a consistent direction or theme. Specifically, straight lines
  • create a sense of structure and formality within the garment, which is a
  • key component of the overall aesthetic. For unity to be achieved, these
  • straight lines must work together and not against each other or other
  • design elements, ensuring every part of the design supports the
  • garment's purpose and overall aesthetic.

questions.question: Differentiate between Hue and Chroma.
questions.solution_html:
• ANSWER: Hue is the property that defines the pure, basic color itself
  • giving the color its name, such as red, blue, or green; it essentially
  • corresponds to the color's position on the traditional color spectrum
  • remaining constant regardless of whether the color is lightened or
  • darkened. The term 'hue' tells you nothing about the color's vividness or
  • how much gray it contains, focusing solely on the pure wavelength of light
  • being perceived, and is the foundational element upon which all other
  • color properties are built.
  • Conversely, Chroma defines a color's purity, intensity, or saturation
  • quantifying how bright, vivid, or free from gray a particular hue is. A color
  • with high chroma is vibrant and pure (e.g., a rich, saturated blue), whereas
  • a color with low chroma appears duller, muted, or closer to neutral gray
  • (e.g., a desaturated, dusty blue), and is the key factor used by designers to
  • create visual contrast and focal points in an outfit.
questions.final_answer: create visual contrast and focal points in an outfit
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Explain the challenges faced by ready to wear industry.
questions.solution_html:
• ANSWER: The Ready-to-Wear apparel industry currently faces
  • significant challenges, primarily driven by the Fast Fashion business
  • model. This model has intensified environmental issues like massive
  • water pollution and textile waste, while also creating supply chain
  • pressures that demand extreme speed and agility, often at the expense of
  • quality and ethical labor practices. Economically, the industry is battling
  • fierce price competition, complex inventory management issues
  • resulting in frequent overproduction, and the struggle to meet consumer
  • demands for both affordability and sustainability.
questions.final_answer: demands for both affordability and sustainability
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Define the terms Classic and Fad in fashion with suitable examples.
questions.solution_html:
• examples.
  • ANSWER: A Classic is a style that possesses a timeless appeal and
  • endures over a long period, remaining consistently fashionable due to its
  • enduring elegance and simplicity, such as the little black dress or a crisp
  • white shirt.
  • In contrast, a Fad is a temporary, popular trend that gains rapid and
  • widespread popularity but has a very short lifespan, quickly rising and
  • then declining just as fast, with examples including baggy trousers or
  • harem pants.

questions.question: Describe the use of colour in creating Emphasis.
questions.solution_html:
• ANSWER: The use of color is a critical method for creating Emphasis
  • in fashion design, as it functions to establish a focal point that captures
  • and holds the viewer's attention. This is primarily achieved through
  • contrast. By using colors that stand out against the surrounding areas
  • such as a contrasting color or a highly saturated hue designers can make
  • a specific part of the garment dominant in the visual hierarchy. For
  • example, color contrast can be effectively used to emphasize the face
  • area, which is the most unique and individualistic part of a person. Color
  • is also instrumental in defining the Dominant elements (most visual
  • weight) and Subordinate elements (least visual weight) of a design.
questions.final_answer: weight) and Subordinate elements (least visual weight) of a design

questions.question: Describe about Color theory.
questions.solution_html:
• ANSWER: Color Theory is a body of guiding principles used to
  • understand the visual effects of specific color combinations and the rules
  • of color mixing. All color is based on light and is organized visually
  • using the Color Wheel. Every color is defined by three main properties
  • Hue (the pure color name, like red), Value (the lightness or darkness of
  • the color), and Chroma (the purity or intensity of the color). Designers
  • use these principles to select harmonious color schemes that evoke a
  • specific mood or feeling in a design.
questions.final_answer: specific mood or feeling in a design

questions.question: List and briefly describe three types of Forms commonly used in Design or Fashion.
questions.solution_html:
• List and briefly describe three types of Forms commonly used
  • in Design or Fashion.
  • ANSWER: The three forms commonly used in design and fashion
  • describe an object's three-dimensional nature (length, width, and
  • depth) and are categorized by their visual characteristics
  • Geometric Forms are precise, mathematical, and characterized by
  • straight lines and sharp corners, creating structured silhouettes like A
  • lines or rectangles.
  • Organic Forms are irregular, curved, and free-flowing, reflecting
  • shapes found in nature, and are used to create fluid, soft, or draped
  • garments like cowl necklines.
  • Abstract Forms are a more complex and conceptual category that
  • simplifies or distorts natural forms for artistic expression, often
  • resulting in highly stylized, non-literal, or avant-garde fashion
  • silhouettes.

questions.question: Explain the classification of Costumes into Traditional, National and Ceremonial types with examples.
questions.solution_html:
• and Ceremonial types with examples.
  • ANSWER: The different types of cultural clothing can be grouped based
  • on their context and function, reflecting a group's heritage, identity, or
  • ceremonial needs.
  • Traditional Costumes, such as the Indian sari, Japanese kimono, Scottish
  • kilt, and Mexican huipil, are outfits that represent the cultural heritage and
  • customs of a specific group or region, often having been worn in daily life
  • in the past or reserved for cultural festivals today.
  • National Costumes are specific outfits, often drawn from traditional wear
  • like India's Sari and Kurta Pajama or the Scottish Kilt, that are recognized
  • as official symbols of a nation or ethnic group, serving as a unifying
  • identity and typically worn on important occasions like national days.
  • Ceremonial Costumes are special clothes, such as an Indian bridal saree, a
  • Christian wedding gown, or the Kathakali dance costume, that are worn
  • only during specific important rituals, formal occasions, or religious
  • events and are imbued with symbolic meaning relevant to the ceremony
  • itself.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Explain in detail rhythm in the context of design Principles.
questions.solution_html:
• ANSWER: The principle of Rhythm in design refers to the visual
  • movement created by the repetition or arrangement of design elements
  • such as colour, line, or texture within a garment. Its primary function is
  • to guide the viewer's eye smoothly and purposefully across the entire
  • outfit, creating a sense of flow, energy, and continuity. By creating
  • tempo and pattern, rhythm ensures the design is dynamic and
  • aesthetically pleasing.
  • Rhythm can be established through various techniques and
  • arrangements
  • • Repetitive Rhythm (Regular Rhythm): This is the most basic and
  • common type, involving the repeated use of a design element like
  • a motif, shapes, pleats, trims, or a consistent colour throughout
  • the garment.
  • • Alternation Rhythm: This occurs when two or more elements are
  • repeated in a regular, alternating pattern, adding visual interest
  • and variety to the design without disrupting balance.
  • • Progressive Rhythm (Gradation): This technique creates rhythm
  • through a gradual increase or decrease in a design element, such
  • as a change in size, colour, shape, or spacing, which draws the
  • eye in a smooth, directional way from one part of the garment to
  • another.
  • • Transition Rhythm: Achieved through the smooth and
  • continuous flow between different elements, often utilizing
  • curved lines, soft draping, or a gradual blending of colours (such
  • as ombré fabric) to move the eye naturally across the garment.
  • • Fluid or Flowing Rhythm: This is created by the harmony of
  • related curves and folds that lead the eye effortlessly throughout
  • the entire costume, with skilful draping, such as in a sari, being a
  • typical example.
  • • Broken or Random Rhythm: Broken or random rhythm occurs
  • when design elements are repeated in an irregular, unexpected, or
  • scattered way. Unlike repetition or alternation, this type of rhythm
  • does not follow a predictable pattern. It creates a sense of surprise
  • modernity, or artistic flair.
  • AMANDA SIMON
  • Assistant Professor
  • KMM College of Arts and Science, Thrikkakara
questions.final_answer: KMM College of Arts and Science, Thrikkakara

  • a color with low chroma appears duller, muted, or closer to neutral gray
  • (e.g., a desaturated, dusty blue), and is the key factor used by designers to
  • create visual contrast and focal points in an outfit.
questions.final_answer: create visual contrast and focal points in an outfit

questions.question: Explain the challenges faced by ready to wear industry.

  • significant challenges, primarily driven by the Fast Fashion business
  • model. This model has intensified environmental issues like massive

  • pressures that demand extreme speed and agility, often at the expense of
  • quality and ethical labor practices. Economically, the industry is battling
  • fierce price competition, complex inventory management issues
  • resulting in frequent overproduction, and the struggle to meet consumer
  • demands for both affordability and sustainability.

questions.question: Describe about Color theory.
questions.solution_html:

  • understand the visual effects of specific color combinations and the rules
  • of color mixing. All color is based on light and is organized visually

  • Hue (the pure color name, like red), Value (the lightness or darkness of
  • the color), and Chroma (the purity or intensity of the color). Designers
  • use these principles to select harmonious color schemes that evoke a
  • specific mood or feeling in a design.

  • in Design or Fashion.
  • ANSWER: The three forms commonly used in design and fashion
  • describe an object's three-dimensional nature (length, width, and
  • depth) and are categorized by their visual characteristics
  • Geometric Forms are precise, mathematical, and characterized by
  • straight lines and sharp corners, creating structured silhouettes like A
  • lines or rectangles.
  • Organic Forms are irregular, curved, and free-flowing, reflecting
  • shapes found in nature, and are used to create fluid, soft, or draped
  • garments like cowl necklines.
  • Abstract Forms are a more complex and conceptual category that
  • simplifies or distorts natural forms for artistic expression, often
  • resulting in highly stylized, non-literal, or avant-garde fashion
  • silhouettes.

questions.question: Explain the classification of Costumes into Traditional, National and Ceremonial types with examples.
questions.solution_html:
• and Ceremonial types with examples.
  • ANSWER: The different types of cultural clothing can be grouped based
  • on their context and function, reflecting a group's heritage, identity, or
  • ceremonial needs.
  • Traditional Costumes, such as the Indian sari, Japanese kimono, Scottish
  • kilt, and Mexican huipil, are outfits that represent the cultural heritage and
  • customs of a specific group or region, often having been worn in daily life
  • in the past or reserved for cultural festivals today.
  • National Costumes are specific outfits, often drawn from traditional wear
  • like India's Sari and Kurta Pajama or the Scottish Kilt, that are recognized
  • as official symbols of a nation or ethnic group, serving as a unifying
  • identity and typically worn on important occasions like national days.
  • Ceremonial Costumes are special clothes, such as an Indian bridal saree, a
  • Christian wedding gown, or the Kathakali dance costume, that are worn
  • only during specific important rituals, formal occasions, or religious
  • events and are imbued with symbolic meaning relevant to the ceremony
  • itself.

questions.question: Explain in detail rhythm in the context of design Principles.
questions.solution_html:
• ANSWER: The principle of Rhythm in design refers to the visual
  • movement created by the repetition or arrangement of design elements
  • such as colour, line, or texture within a garment. Its primary function is
  • to guide the viewer's eye smoothly and purposefully across the entire
  • outfit, creating a sense of flow, energy, and continuity. By creating
  • tempo and pattern, rhythm ensures the design is dynamic and
  • aesthetically pleasing.
  • Rhythm can be established through various techniques and
  • arrangements
  • • Repetitive Rhythm (Regular Rhythm): This is the most basic and
  • common type, involving the repeated use of a design element like
  • a motif, shapes, pleats, trims, or a consistent colour throughout
  • the garment.
  • • Alternation Rhythm: This occurs when two or more elements are
  • repeated in a regular, alternating pattern, adding visual interest
  • and variety to the design without disrupting balance.
  • • Progressive Rhythm (Gradation): This technique creates rhythm
  • through a gradual increase or decrease in a design element, such
  • as a change in size, colour, shape, or spacing, which draws the
  • eye in a smooth, directional way from one part of the garment to
  • another.
  • • Transition Rhythm: Achieved through the smooth and
  • continuous flow between different elements, often utilizing
  • curved lines, soft draping, or a gradual blending of colours (such
  • as ombré fabric) to move the eye naturally across the garment.
  • • Fluid or Flowing Rhythm: This is created by the harmony of
  • related curves and folds that lead the eye effortlessly throughout
  • the entire costume, with skilful draping, such as in a sari, being a
  • typical example.
  • • Broken or Random Rhythm: Broken or random rhythm occurs
  • when design elements are repeated in an irregular, unexpected, or
  • scattered way. Unlike repetition or alternation, this type of rhythm
  • does not follow a predictable pattern. It creates a sense of surprise
  • modernity, or artistic flair.
  • AMANDA SIMON
  • Assistant Professor
  • KMM College of Arts and Science, Thrikkakara
